procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent, Bishwanath Prasad, filed a petition under Arts. 226 and 227 of the Constitution before the Patna High Court challenging the award inter alia on the ground that the Labour Court had failed to appreciate that the enquiry officer had acted malafide and in violation of the principles of natural justice in holding the enquiry. A complaint was also made that the letters Workmen (1) the High Court took the view that it was necessary for the Labour Court to first go into the question whether or not there was a conciliation proceeding pending at the date when the dismissal order was made with a view to find out whether the plea of the workmen concerned that the impugned order of dismissal was -pas~d in contravention of s. 33 (2) (b) was correct or not and if it accepted the petitioner's conten-tion that the order of dismissal contravened s. 33 (2) (b), •,the departmental enquiry would. not avail the employer and the whole question would be open. The High Court directed that the petitioner should be afforded an opportunity to place the letters earlier referred to, , viz., annexures I and I-1, and such other relevant evidence in this connection as he might choose before the .Labour Court and the Labour Court should come to its own conclusion on the issue before it upon all the evidence adduced before it. Being of the view that in the absence of any determination of the basic question whether or not there was a contravention of s. 33, the High Court did not think it advisable to pronounce upon the merit.s of the several contentions raised on behalf of the peti-tioner, set aside the award and remitted the matter back to the Labour Court for making a fresh award in accordance with the court's observations.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and upheld the award of the Labour Court, finding that the High Court's order remitting the matter back to the Labour Court was not justified.

directions: The award of the Labour Court is upheld.
The order for costs made at the time when special leave was granted in this case will stand.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order of dismissal passed in contravention of Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is automatically invalid and ineffective, rendering the domestic enquiry held by the employer of no avail.

facts: A workman was dismissed following a domestic enquiry. The workman contended that the dismissal order was passed in contravention of Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
The issue was whether this alleged contravention automatically made the dismissal invalid and the domestic enquiry of no avail.

The dispute was referred to a Labour Court, which upheld the dismissal on its merits. The High Court, however, took the view that if a contravention of Section 33 was found, the domestic enquiry would not avail the employer and the whole matter would be open for fresh adjudication.
law: The Supreme Court clarified that the ban on dismissal imposed by Section 33 is a procedural safeguard. Getting permission under Section 33 merely removes the ban; it does not automatically validate the dismissal.
A dismissal made in disregard of the ban in Section 33 is not automatically void or inoperative.

Section 33A allows an employee dismissed in contravention of Section 33 to file a complaint, which the Labour Court or Tribunal must then adjudicate as if it were an industrial dispute referred under Section 10.
There is no requirement that a Labour Court or Tribunal must order reinstatement as soon as it finds a violation of Section 33.
application: The Court explained that when a complaint is filed under Section 33A (or a dispute is referred under Section 10) alleging a violation of Section 33, the Tribunal's duty is not just to check for the procedural violation but to adjudicate the dispute on its merits.
Even if a contravention of Section 33 is established, the employer is entitled to justify the dismissal on its merits by adducing evidence before the Tribunal.

The Tribunal must examine the substance of the case, including whether the employer acted in good faith, without victimization or unfair labour practice, and whether the findings of the domestic enquiry were perverse or based on a violation of natural justice.
Therefore, the domestic enquiry is not automatically rendered of no avail. The employer can still rely on it, and the Tribunal will assess its validity and the justification for the dismissal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that an order of dismissal passed in contravention of Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act is not automatically invalid or ineffective. The violation does not render the domestic enquiry of no avail; instead, it allows the workman to bring the dispute before a Labour Court or Tribunal, where the employer has the right to justify the dismissal on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Labour Court must first determine if there was a contravention of Section 33 of the Act before considering the merits of the dismissal.

facts: A workman challenged his dismissal, arguing it contravened Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act.
The High Court held that the Labour Court must first decide the preliminary issue of whether Section 33 was contravened.
The High Court believed that if a contravention was found, the employer's internal departmental enquiry would be irrelevant, and the whole case would be open for adjudication.
law: Section 33A of the Act allows a workman to file a complaint if an employer violates Section 33.
When such a complaint is filed, the Labour Court or Tribunal must adjudicate it as if it were a full industrial dispute referred to it under Section 10.
A violation of the ban in Section 33 does not automatically render the dismissal void or inoperative; it merely removes the procedural ban.
It is well-settled that even if a dismissal contravenes Section 33, the employer is entitled to justify the dismissal on its merits by adducing evidence before the Tribunal.
application: The Supreme Court explained that the purpose of Section 33A is to provide a workman with a direct remedy, treating the complaint as a full-fledged industrial dispute.
Therefore, the scope of the inquiry under Section 33A is not limited to just the contravention but also includes the merits of the dismissal itself.
The Court explicitly stated that the law does not require a Tribunal to award reinstatement as soon as it finds a violation of Section 33.
Instead, the Tribunal must proceed to examine the merits of the case, just as it would in a dispute referred under Section 10. This involves allowing the employer to justify its action.
The Court concluded that whether the case is a complaint under Section 33A or a reference under Section 10, the Tribunal must deal with both the contravention and the merits of the dismissal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's position, holding that a Labour Court is not required to first determine the issue of a Section 33 contravention as a preliminary matter. Instead, the Tribunal must adjudicate the entire complaint, which includes not only the question of contravention but also the merits of the dismissal, allowing the employer to justify its action with evidence.

issue.issue_text: In an adjudication concerning a dismissal, whether the Tribunal's inquiry, even if a contravention of Section 33 is alleged, must still consider if the employer's action was justified on its merits, including examining for bad faith, victimisation, unfair labour practice, and procedural fairness of the domestic enquiry.

law.fact: Under Section 33A, if an employer contravenes Section 33 (which restricts dismissal during pendency of proceedings), an employee can file a complaint which the Tribunal must adjudicate as if it were a referred industrial dispute.

law.fact: When reviewing a dismissal for misconduct, a Tribunal will interfere if there is a want of good faith, victimisation, unfair labour practice, a basic error or violation of natural justice, or if the finding is baseless or perverse.
law.snippet: In case of dismissal on misconduct, the Tribunal does not, however, act as a Court of appeal and substitute its own judgment for that of the manage- ment. It will interfere (i) when there is a want of good faith, (ii) when there is victimisation or unfair labour practice, (iii) when the manage- ment has been guilty of a basic error or violation of a principle of natural justice, and (iv) when on the materials the finding is completely baseless or perverse.'

application.fact: The Court established that even if a dismissal contravenes Section 33, the employer is still permitted to justify the dismissal on its merits by providing evidence to the Tribunal.
application.snippet: It is well settled that if an application is made by an employee under s. 33A and it is shown that the impugned.-dismissal of the employee has contravened s. 33, it is open to the employer to justify the dis- missal on the merits by adducing satisfactory evi- dence before the Tribunal.

application.fact: The Court clarified that a finding of a Section 33 violation does not automatically result in reinstatement for the employee, as the merits must still be considered.
application.snippet: These sections do not require that as soon as the Labour Court or Tribunal finds that there has been a violation of s. 33 it should award reinstatement.

application.fact: The Court reasoned that whether a case is brought under Section 33A (as a complaint) or Section 10 (as a reference), the Tribunal's duty is the same: it must decide on the alleged contravention and also on the merits of the dismissal.
application.snippet: There can be no doubt that if under a complaint filed untler s. 33A a tribunal has to deal not only with the question of contravention but also with the merits of the order of dismissal, the position· cannot be any different when a reference is made to ... the tribunal like the present under s. 10.

application.fact: The Court affirmed that the Tribunal's inquiry into the merits must include an examination of whether the employer's action was justified, specifically checking for bad faith, victimisation, unfair labour practices, and procedural flaws in the domestic inquiry.
application.snippet: The Labour Court would still have to consider whether the employer's action was justified and would have to be satisfied that the allegations about want of good faith or victimisation or unfair Jabour practice were baseless, that the inquiry was not vitiated by basic errors or violation of any principles of natural justice, and that the order of dismissal was not perverse.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Tribunal's inquiry cannot be limited to determining whether a contravention of Section 33 occurred. Even if such a violation is found, it does not conclude the matter. The Tribunal must proceed to adjudicate the dispute on its merits, which requires the employer to justify the dismissal. This involves the Tribunal examining the action for want of good faith, victimisation, unfair labour practice, and ensuring the domestic inquiry was procedurally fair and its findings were not perverse.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order of dismissal passed in contravention of Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is automatically invalid and ineffective, rendering the domestic enquiry held by the employer of no avail.
appellant_arguments: A contravention of Section 33 does not automatically invalidate a dismissal order; the merits of the dismissal must still be adjudicated.
The pendency of conciliation proceedings at the time of discharge does not affect the merits of the question of whether the dismissal was justified.
respondent_arguments: If an order of dismissal contravenes Section 33, the departmental enquiry would not avail the employer, and the whole question would be open before the Labour Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Labour Court must first determine if there was a contravention of Section 33 of the Act before considering the merits of the dismissal.
appellant_arguments: The Labour Court's primary duty is to adjudicate the dispute on its merits, and it is not required to decide the issue of a Section 33 contravention as a preliminary matter.
respondent_arguments: It is necessary for the Labour Court to first decide the 'basic question' of whether there was a contravention of Section 33 before pronouncing upon the merits of the dismissal.

arguments.issue_text: In an adjudication concerning a dismissal, whether the Tribunal's inquiry, even if a contravention of Section 33 is alleged, must still consider if the employer's action was justified on its merits, including examining for bad faith, victimisation, unfair labour practice, and procedural fairness of the domestic enquiry.
appellant_arguments: The Labour Court's primary role is to adjudicate the dispute referred to it, which requires going into the question of whether the employee was properly dismissed on the merits.

The Labour Court correctly examined the evidence and found that the employee's action was subversive of discipline and merited dismissal, and no grounds like bad faith or victimisation were substantiated.
respondent_arguments: The merits of the dismissal should not be considered until the preliminary question of a Section 33 contravention is determined, as a contravention would render the employer's enquiry invalid.

cases.case_name: Indian Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. v. Their Workmen
cases.principle: It formulates the principles for a Labour Court to follow when examining the merits of a management's decision to dismiss a workman.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Labour Court must uphold an employer's dismissal of an employee for an act that is subversive of discipline, such as lodging a false complaint against company officers, unless it is substantiated that the employer's action was a result of want of good faith, victimisation, unfair labour practice, or that the internal enquiry was vitiated by a basic error, a violation of natural justice, or its findings were perverse.
obiter: The pendency of a conciliation proceeding does not alter the requirement for a Tribunal to assess whether an employer's action was justified based on established legal principles.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A contravention of the ban in Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, does not render an employer's dismissal order automatically void or inoperative. In an industrial dispute referred for adjudication under Section 10, the tribunal's primary duty is to decide the dispute on its merits. The question of a Section 33 contravention is merely one point to be decided and does not conclude the inquiry; the tribunal must still proceed to consider whether the dismissal was otherwise justified based on the evidence and established principles.
legal_tests_applied: In adjudicating a dismissal, the Tribunal must be satisfied that allegations of want of good faith, victimisation, or unfair labour practice are baseless. The Tribunal must also be satisfied that the domestic enquiry was not vitiated by a basic error or violation of any principle of natural justice, and that the finding on which the order of dismissal was passed was not perverse or without any foundation.
policy_considerations: What is referred to the tribunal under Section 10 is the entire industrial dispute between the employer and its employees. While an alleged contravention of Section 33 is a point the tribunal must decide, the decision on this question does not conclude the enquiry. The tribunal's fundamental task is to consider if the dismissal orders are justified and whether reinstatement is appropriate after considering all relevant aspects of the case, in order to make an appropriate award that adequately deals with the referred dispute.
